EAMS / Research
Research

What we work on

Department research is organized around five thematic areas and is carried out through six named labs and centers. Faculty regularly cross between areas; almost every active project has at least one secondary affiliation.

Research areas

Coastal Resilience

The largest thematic area in the department, anchored by the Cobbett Bay observing system. Faculty work across the spectrum from physical drivers (sea-level rise, storm surge, sediment supply) to ecological response (marsh stability, intertidal communities) to municipal adaptation planning. The recent Nature Geoscience AMOC paper grew out of this group.

Featured labs

  • AMOC & Western Boundary Group
  • Cobbett Marsh Observatory
  • Salt Marsh Geomorphology Lab

Atmospheric Chemistry

EAMS atmospheric chemists operate one of the most heavily instrumented coastal-aerosol observatories on the US East Coast. Research spans gas-phase chemistry (NOx, ozone, VOCs), aerosol-cloud interactions, and the photochemistry of dissolved organic matter at the air-sea interface. The group runs a shared mass-spectrometry suite that is open to graduate students across the department.

Paleoclimate

The paleoclimate group reconstructs Holocene and Pleistocene climate from lakes, marine sediments, ice cores, and cosmogenic-nuclide-dated landforms. The Rasmussen group's eight-thousand-year varve record from Lake Atticut anchors a regional reconstruction of northeastern US drought variability. The glaciology subgroup runs ongoing fieldwork in southeast Greenland.

Featured labs

  • Lake Sediment & Isotope Lab
  • Glaciology Group
  • Cosmogenic Nuclide Lab (shared)

Affiliated faculty

  • Rasmussen
  • Two-Hawk (S.)
  • Kowalczyk

Marine Ecology

The marine ecology group studies community-level responses of cold-temperate marine systems to disturbance — marine heatwaves, eutrophication recovery, and the long-running northward range expansion of southern species. The 22-year intertidal time series anchors much of the group's work. Most students do at least one field season at the Cobbett Marine Laboratory.

  • Plankton Dynamics Group
  • Polar Oceanography Lab

Earth Systems Modeling

A cross-cutting area that includes numerical modeling of geodynamics, atmospheric and ocean dynamics, and machine-learning approaches to earth-system data. The group runs the tectos high-performance computing cluster (1,200 cores; 4.8 PB scratch storage) and coordinates the department's contribution to the Community Earth System Model.

Centers and labs

Most named labs occupy dedicated space in Mendel Hall; the Cobbett Marine Laboratory is housed in a separate department-owned building on Cobbett Point, 25 minutes from main campus by department shuttle.

Cobbett Marine Laboratory

Director: Prof. Volponi · Cobbett Point, MA

The department's coastal marine field station, including dock facilities for the R/V Cobbett Bay, a 60-seat seminar room, a flow-through seawater system, and ten faculty-and-student labs. Open year-round.

Coastal Aerosol Observatory

PI: Prof. Adeyemi · Cobbett Point + 3 satellite stations

Four-station instrumented coastal aerosol observatory, with continuous measurements of size distribution, composition, and optical properties. Data are publicly served through the EAMS open-data portal with a 6-month embargo.

Lake Sediment & Isotope Lab

PI: Prof. Rasmussen · M-322 Mendel Hall

The department's lake-coring and paleoclimate laboratory, including dedicated GC-IRMS and TIMS instruments, a refrigerated core archive, and a varve-counting microscope suite. Holds 1,800+ archived cores from across the northeastern US and the North Atlantic islands.

Hartwell Mass Spectrometry Facility

Director: Min Shao, RS · M-503 Mendel Hall

Shared facility housing the department's high-resolution AMS, a soft-ionization CIMS, a multi-collector ICP-MS, and three GC-IRMS instruments. Open to all EAMS investigators and external academic users.

Cobbett Marsh Observatory

PI: Prof. Arroyo · Cobbett Marsh, MA

Long-term study site for salt-marsh dynamics, in operation since 2009. Continuous monitoring of tides, water level, sediment accretion, salinity, and vegetation composition at three transects. Co-managed with The Trustees of Reservations.

Mineral Physics Lab

PI: Prof. McAllister · M-406 Mendel Hall

High-pressure mineral physics laboratory equipped with two diamond-anvil cells, a Raman microspectrometer, and shared time on the Argonne synchrotron. Focused on lower-mantle phase relations and the deep-Earth water cycle.
